digest.intro: Hexagons on Mars, hollowed-out institutions, and a war nobody named.

items.title: Peer Review Is Buckling — and AI Is Only Part of the Problem
items.blurb: A health economist's paper on HPV vaccine mandates was rejected by a single reviewer who confused vaccine efficacy with policy effectiveness — two entirely different questions. Peer review's structural problem isn't dishonesty but collapse-by-volume: submissions have outrun the supply of willing, careful reviewers, so journals are accepting one-reviewer verdicts and AI-assisted reviews that pass superficially but miss the point. The knowledge-verification layer of science is quietly failing, and almost nobody outside the system is tracking it.

items.title: What Happened to HackerOne
items.blurb: In 2011, two hackers cold-emailed 100 tech giants, found bugs in Google, Facebook, and Apple, and built HackerOne to make ethical security research less legally terrifying. A decade later, the person who managed large bug bounty programs on both sides of that relationship describes a textbook arc: community trust traded for enterprise contracts, incentive structures quietly inverted, institutional memory gone. It's a story about what happens when a platform built on hacker values starts optimizing for a different customer.

items.title: AI for Science Needs Reasoning, Not Just Data
items.blurb: AlphaFold solved a fifty-year-old protein structure problem by pattern-matching against known shapes — impressive, but it doesn't generalize to science that lacks large training sets or requires genuine hypothesis generation. The argument here is that what's missing isn't more data or bigger models but reasoning: the ability to model the actual epistemic process of research, including knowing when you don't know. Pairs uncomfortably well with the peer review collapse story above.

sections.heading: Geometry, deep time, and the shape of things

items.title: Mount Toba Didn't Almost Kill Us — New Lake Sediment Data Rewrites the Story
items.blurb: 74,000 years ago, Toba erupted with roughly 1,000 times the force of Pinatubo — and textbooks have said ever since that it nearly wiped out humanity. New sediment cores from a crater lake on the Kenya-Tanzania border show the cooling lasted under two years and amounted to maybe half a degree. The twist is physical: above a certain eruption size, aerosol droplets become too heavy and settle out of the stratosphere too quickly to sustain a volcanic winter, which means the biggest eruptions are paradoxically less catastrophic than mid-sized ones.

items.title: Even on Mars, Hexagons Are the Bestagons
items.blurb: NASA's Curiosity rover is rolling through a vast field of hexagonal polygonal fractures in Valle Grande — and the honest answer is nobody knows exactly how they formed. Dried mud, freeze-thaw cycling, and ancient hydrology are all on the table, which makes this both an open scientific question and a clue about Mars's geologically recent past. The field stretches as far as the camera sees: the same tiling pattern that falls out of soap bubbles, basalt columns, and Saturn's pole, now confirmed on another planet's surface.

items.title: Europe's Oldest Buddhist Temple, Built to Honor Napoleon's Enemies
items.blurb: The Khosheutovsky Khurul sits on the Russian steppe as an architectural object that shouldn't exist — a Buddhist temple built in 1817 to commemorate a Kalmyk cavalry regiment that fought alongside Russian forces against Napoleon. Aeon's video essays consistently find the place where military history, diaspora identity, and sacred architecture collide; this one is built around an object that is simultaneously a war memorial, a religious site, and a relic of a nomadic people's survival across empires.

items.title: Someone Is Bulk-Buying 5,000 Obscure Books from European Independents — Nobody Knows Why
items.blurb: Orders of 5,000 titles are arriving overnight at independent booksellers from Galway to Berlin — no haggling, €10,000–€50,000 a pop, mixing A History of Connemara with a 2018 driving test guide. The booksellers are cashing in but quietly terrified: a similar pattern swept US antiquarian dealers earlier this year, and the working theory is that someone is systematically sweeping physical copies of long-tail titles off the market, possibly to corner bibliographic scarcity. The motive — archival, speculative, adversarial — remains genuinely unknown.

facts.fact: Out of 443 occupations on nearly 9 million US death certificates, taxi and ambulance drivers had the lowest rate of dying from Alzheimer's disease — roughly 1 in 100, versus 1 in 60 overall.

The Mount Toba eruption 74,000 years ago — roughly 1,000 times larger than Pinatubo — appears to have caused less than half a degree of global cooling lasting under two years, not the near-extinction volcanic winter long theorized.

make_something.prompt: Take the Martian hexagonal fracture fields as a starting texture system: write a WebGL shader or generative sketch that tiles a surface with Voronoi-relaxed hexagons, then introduces a slow freeze-thaw deformation cycle — vertices drifting, cracks widening and healing — as if the geometry is trying to decide whether it's mud, ice, or regolith. The constraint: the only inputs are time and a single noise seed. No color, just topology and crack width.

art_picks.title: Sans Soleil
art_picks.creator: Chris Marker
art_picks.why: A film built like an essay built like a memory — Marker cuts between Tokyo rituals, Cape Verde villages, and Icelandic lava to ask how images construct time and culture. The systems question underneath: how do societies encode meaning into objects and ceremony? Devastating and generative.

art_picks.title: Flatlands
art_picks.creator: Casey Reas
art_picks.why: Reas has spent 25 years treating code as a drawing instrument — not visualization, but mark-making with probability and rule-sets. His work sits exactly at the edge where software becomes expressive self-portrait, and the tension between control and emergence is the whole subject.

art_picks.title: Selected Ambient Works Volume II
art_picks.creator: Aphex Twin
art_picks.why: Not ambient as background — ambient as a system for constructing interior states. Each piece functions like a different light condition in an empty room. The obsessive craft is in the negative space: what's withheld, what's left to the listener's nervous system to complete.

events.name: Oren Fischer: HALLEL in collaboration with Havurah
events.why: A show built around ritual text and communal practice — art that functions as community and liturgy simultaneously, blurring the boundary between sacred form and contemporary installation in a small TriBeCa space worth the detour.

events.name: Greater New York 2026
events.venue: MoMA PS1, 22-25 Jackson Ave, Long Island City, Queens
events.why: The quinquennial survey of 53 NYC-area early-career artists — site-specific commissions spanning the whole building, organized around surveillance, economic precarity, and shifting technologies — closes this Sunday; it's genuinely the last call.

events.name: Whitney Biennial 2026 (82nd Edition)
events.venue: Whitney Museum of American Art, 99 Gansevoort St, Manhattan
events.why: The 82nd Biennial — curated by Marcela Guerrero and Drew Sawyer — closes Aug 23; if you haven't gone, this is the final two-week window on what's been called the must-see survey show of 2026.

events.name: Lily van der Stokker: Male Art Exhibition, Great Show
events.why: Van der Stokker's work is deceptively cheerful — pastel, domestic, self-deprecating — but the subject is always the ideological weight of taste, gender, and art-world status; expressive surface with structural critique underneath.

events.name: Warm Up 2026 — Fridays Aug 14 & 21
events.venue: MoMA PS1 Courtyard, 22-25 Jackson Ave, Long Island City, Queens
events.why: Two Fridays left of the 28th season: an outdoor electronic music series curated as part of PS1's art program — drawing from dub, techno, gabber, house, and avant-garde improvisation — with the museum galleries open late alongside it.
